UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                     )
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                         )           Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                     )
                                                     )
                                                     )

                                      ANSWER OF VISTRA CORP.

          Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby moves to answer certain

pleadings and answers filed in the above-captioned proceeding. As the timely-filed comments in

this proceeding nearly universally agree, IRAS has not been shown to be just and reasonable and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Although PJM stakeholders may disagree about the best

way to address resource adequacy concerns in PJM, there is nearly unanimous consensus—

amongst Load Serving Entities (“LSE”), independent power producers, vertically integrated

utilities, end-use customers, state public utility commissions, individual retail ratepayers, and

PJM’s Independent Market Monitor—that PJM’s Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”)

proposal is not the way forward.

          It should be no surprise that IRAS has elicited such strong opposition. Nor should it be a

surprise that its defenders have not put forth a convincing case in support of the proposal. To start,

PJM has misdiagnosed the root cause of the region’s resource adequacy issues. PJM blames large

loads rather than recognizing a combination of exaggerated load forecasts and capacity auction

and interconnection delays that contribute significantly to the resource adequacy gap. To the




    1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).
      extent a market participant is contributing to the resource adequacy gap, it is LSEs and Electric

     Distributors (“EDs”) that commit to load that they do not have the capacity to support. Addressing

     PJM’s resource adequacy quandary by penalizing large loads under IRAS’s discriminatory and ill-

     fitting framework is fraught with risk. From there, PJM compounds its initial error by offering a

     solution that is illegal for several independent reasons. Finally, IRAS threatens to have the exact

     opposite effect PJM intends. It will make the resource adequacy situation more dire because its

     failure to include common-sense transition mechanisms and grandfathering provisions will upend

     investments made in reliance on the existing market rules, thereby chilling additional investment

     in the PJM region.

I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

              Although the Commission’s procedural rules generally do not allow answers to answers,

     the Commission may permit them for good cause. 2 The Commission frequently accepts answers

     that clarify the issues before the Commission, ensure a complete record, or otherwise assist the

     Commission in its decision-making.3 Vistra therefore respectfully requests that the Commission

     accept this answer, which will assist the Commission with its decision-making by contextualizing

     the record, responding to answers, and explaining why the scant support for IRAS is misplaced.




         2
          18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument, or
     a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”).
         3
           See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 182 FERC ¶ 61,073, at P 13 (2023) (accepting answers to answers that
     “provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process”); New Fortress Energy LLC, 174 FERC
     61,207, at P 7 (2021) (accepting answers because they provided information that assisted the Commission’s
     decisionmaking process); Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting answers that
     “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making”); Saltville Gas Storage
     Co., L.L.C., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in understanding
     the issues raised, and will ensure a complete record”).

                                                                  -2-
 II.   ANSWER

           As the record clearly demonstrates, IRAS has myriad fatal flaws. An order accepting the

  IRAS proposal will not be upheld in court and, in the meantime, will cast a pall of uncertainty over

  the PJM market, stymying investments in both new capacity and the maintenance of existing

  capacity. That, in turn, will further harm PJM’s resource adequacy outlook.

           A. PJM Has Misdiagnosed the Cause of the Region’s Resource Adequacy Issues

           Perhaps the most fundamental of IRAS’s many flaws is that it attempts to solve the wrong

  problem. As parties in this proceeding have now demonstrated in several different ways, the

  source of PJM’s resource adequacy woes is the incentive structure that PJM’s capacity market

  creates: incentivizing LSEs to agree to serve more load than they have generation to cover or can

  realistically procure through the capacity market. 4 When the PJM system had excess generation

  and the capacity price was clearing at or below $50/MW-day, this was an entirely rational and

  efficient strategy. That became particularly problematic in this period of rapid load growth

  because LSEs currently have every incentive to sign up as much load as possible without r egard

  to whether they have sufficient supply to serve that load, and that dynamic is only made worse in

  today’s supply-constrained environment. “Net-short LSEs” signing up unlimited customers

  without a plan to adequately supply them is a recipe for both resource adequacy shortfalls and

  reliability problems.




      4
        See Dominion Comments at 3-4 (the resource shortfall stems in part from “LSEs relying solely on the BRA”
  rather than bilateral contracting, and that “LSEs should have an affirmative obligation to procure new capacity to
  cover any new Large Loads they seek to interconnect and serve”); East Kentucky Power Cooperative Comments at
  14-15 (“PJM does not propose to evaluate whether an LSE’s supply resource portfolio is sufficient to satisfy aggregate
  load and reliability requirements. . . . PJM does not address whether the LSE is causing the resource adequacy concern
  that IRAS is intended to address. However, it is not just and reasonable to subject to IRAS curtailment the load of an
  LSE that has prudently planned its power supply portfolio to include sufficient resources to meet its load -serving
  obligations, including for New Large Load.”).

                                                               -3-
           Yet PJM has entirely ignored that issue, and the reform that PJM proposes—i.e., assigning

curtailment obligations based on whether an individual retail load offsets its demand with new

capacity—will exacerbate the region’s resource adequacy challenge. Notably, under PJM’s

proposal, an LSE would be curtailed because a new large load in its footprint did not bring new

capacity online even if that LSE planned ahead and has sufficient resources to meet its load -serving

obligations. And, conversely, an LSE that has not procured enough capacity for the load it is

obligated to serve will avoid curtailment as long as the large load in its footprint brought its own

new capacity.        Thus, in the name of solving a resource adequacy shortfall, PJM could

simultaneously curtail entities that have done nothing to cause that shortfall in the first place while

rewarding entities that have signed up more load than they have planned to serve. This problem

will only get worse as resources reach the end of their useful lives and state and federal

environmental regulations begin to bind. The likely wave of resource retirements is the next

significant challenge the PJM system will face. By misidentifying the source of the current

resource shortfall, PJM will hinder the ability to address the next resource adequacy challenge.

          In defending IRAS, Governor Shapiro’s filing claims that “PJM is appropriately aligning

IRAS with existing practices that generally limit curtailment signals to zones with real-time

capacity shortfalls.” 5 But IRAS does not limit curtailments to zones with real-time capacity

shortfalls. Instead, IRAS directs curtailments based on individual retail customers’ contracting

decisions, which is not necessarily indicative of whether a zone or area is resource adequate.

Indeed, a zone or area with a 100 MW capacity surplus that adds a 50 MW Eligible New Large

Load to its footprint would nevertheless be called to curtail 50 MW whenever an IRAS event is




    5
        Gov. Shapiro Answer at 9.

                                                      -4-
 triggered. The notion that the “aggregate MW limitations on service imposed [through IRAS] at

the zonal transmission system-level[] is appropriate and commensurate with the risks posed to the

bulk power system” 6 is misinformed. An ED or LSE that poses no risk to reliability could still be

called to curtail because IRAS is not keyed to wholesale zonal conditions. This, in turn, means

that PJM will curtail LSEs or EDs that are resource adequate while not curtailing LSEs or EDs

that are not resource adequate. That, by definition, will jeopardize reliability in the operational

time horizon and make it more difficult to ensure resource adequacy in the planning horizon. A

“solution” that misidentifies the problem, rewards entities that are ca using the problem, and

punishes entities that are not causing the problem is definitionally unjust, unreasonable, and unduly

discriminatory and preferential.

         The most frustrating element of PJM’s IRAS proposal is that PJM could have designed a

curtailment protocol similar to IRAS but focused on short LSEs. Rather than develop a large load

registry, PJM could have designed a registry where LSEs identify their supply arrangements.

Instead of designating LSEs with large loads for curtailments, PJM could have required short LSEs

to identify loads that would be curtailed when PJM is in an operational emergency. If PJM had

simply targeted the IRAS infrastructure at short LSEs instead of large loads it could have addressed

its near-term challenges in a just and reasonable, not unduly discriminatory, and jurisdictionally

durable fashion.

         B. IRAS Exceeds the Commission’s Jurisdiction

         The record resoundingly demonstrates that IRAS is jurisdictionally impermissible.

Numerous parties have echoed Vistra’s arguments that the proposal targets retail customers, in




   6
       Gov. Shapiro Answer at 4.

                                                     -5-
 violation of the FPA’s jurisdictional boundaries. 7 Although a small handful of parties take the

opposite view, their arguments are flawed, self -defeating, or lack support altogether.

          PJM’s jurisdictional defense stalls in the garage because it fundamentally misunderstands

the controlling Supreme Court precedent. PJM myopically insists that the Supreme Court’s

“targeting” inquiry turns only on the utility’s stated justification for th e rate it is proposing.

Specifically, in PJM’s telling, EPSA instructs that “[w]hether [] a rule ‘targets’ retail or wholesale

customers turns on the justification for the rule, not on whether or the extent to which the rule

affects or even compels action of retail or wholesale customers.” 8 This is wrong. While the Court

in EPSA considered the Commission’s justification for Order No. 745, it did so only after

considering how the rule “work[ed]” and concluding that “whatever the effects at the retail level,

every aspect of the regulatory plan happens exclusively on the wholesale market and governs

exclusively that market’s rules.” 9 So while PJM argues that language in its transmittal confirms

that IRAS is “targeted to PJM’s wholesale market and enhancing the reliable operation of the bulk

electric power system” 10 that is beside the point because, in practice, every aspect of IRAS does

not happen exclusively at the wholesale level. In other words, PJM’s stated target does not match

its reforms’ actual target.

          Contrary to PJM’s position, the jurisdictional inquiry required by the FPA does not turn on

how a utility characterizes a rate in a transmittal letter. If it did, any utility could bend the FPA’s

jurisdictional bright line to its liking based on how it characterized its proposal in the transmittal




    7
        See, e.g., Constellation Comments at 13; Corporate Energy Buyers Association Comments at 7.
    8
        PJM Answer at 19-20 (citing FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 264 (2016) (“EPSA”)).
    9
        EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.
    10
         PJM Answer at 21.

                                                         -6-
 letter. Claiming that up is down does not make it so. The FPA’s jurisdictional divide cannot turn

on how a filer describes its intent in a transmittal letter. The Commission must look at the filed

rate itself and determine whether it targets a matter within the states’ jurisdiction.

           Next, PJM and several other parties contend that, because PJM would not literally curtail

individual retail customers, it cannot be targeting them. 11 But that response entirely misses the

point. PJM is targeting retail customers’ capacity procurement practices and requiring those

customers’ LSEs and EDs to curtail service to those retail customers based on their retail-level

activity. Despite PJM’s argument to the contrary, the stated intent of a regulatory action is not

what matters from a jurisdictional perspective. If PJM were correct, it would have been completely

unnecessary for the Supreme Court to “consider[] ‘the target at which a law aims’” in the first

place.12 The Supreme Court instead could have held that the jurisdictional inquiry turns on “the

stated intent of the law.” But that was not the holding in EPSA or Oneok.

           Thus, it is simply incorrect that “protestors cannot logically claim both that PJM’s proposal

unlawfully ‘targets retail customers’ and that PJM’s proposal is fatally flawed because it cannot

guarantee which individual retail customers are curtailed.” 13 It is true that PJM has targeted retail

customers by proposing to assign load curtailments to EDs and LSEs based on the retail customers

they serve. It is also true that EDs and LSEs assigned curtailment may direct those curtailments

at other end-use customers such that the incentives for large loads to BYONC are undermined.

The fact that PJM’s shot may miss the target does not change where PJM aimed. As the Supreme



    11
     PJM Answer at 26-28; See, e.g., Gov. Shapiro Answer at 9-10 (“[P]rotestors cannot logically claim both that
PJM’s proposal unlawfully ‘targets retail customers’ and that PJM’s proposal is fatally flawed because it cannot
guarantee which individual reta il customers are curtailed. Both cannot be true.”); Appalachian Voices Comments at
8.
    12
         EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282 (quoting Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373, 385 (2015) (“Oneok”)).
    13
         Gov. Shapiro Answer at 9-10.

                                                           -7-
 Court has long recognized, both federal and state regulators can nominally address a matter within

their respective purview while in fact impermissibly targeting or aiming at the other. 14 Doing so

violates the FPA’s bright line between federal and state jurisdiction as much as if the relevant

regulator exceeded its jurisdiction directly. 15           For example, in Hughes, Maryland’s state-

jurisdictional contract-for-differences scheme did not dictate the wholesale auction clearing price

directly. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court held that the scheme was jurisdictionally impermissible

because it guaranteed the generator a rate distinct from the auction clearing price, even though it

did not literally change that price. “That Maryland was attempting to encourage construction of

new in-state generation does not save its program,” because, as the Court put it, the program

amounted to indirect wholesale rate setting that “invade[d] FERC’s regulatory turf.”16 So too here

where PJM has proposed to differentiate customers’ wholesale service based solely on the

practices of retail customers.

          Although certain parties try to frame IRAS as working only at the wholesale level, 17 their

own pleadings prove otherwise. For example, Governor Shapiro’s filing claims that IRAS does

not “[t]arget retail customers . . . by mak[ing] the characteristics of the retail customer . . . th e basis

for a curtailment obligation.” 18 At the same time, Governor Shapiro’s filing asserts that IRAS

would “limit the total MWs of load reduction in a zone or area based on the share of new large

loads . . . that have failed to meet their capacity needs through BYONC or capacity procured

      Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 164 (2016); Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385; N. Nat. Gas Co. v.
State Corp. Comm’n of Kan., 372 U.S. 84, 94 (1963); Nw. Cent. Pipeline Corp. v. State Corp. Com’n of Kan., 489
U.S. 493, 514-15 (1989).
    15
      EPSA, 577 U.S. at 289 (“The FPA leaves no room either for direct state regulation of the prices of interstate
wholesales” or for regulation that “would indirectly achieve the same result.” (internal quotation marks omitted)).
    16
      Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. at 163-64.
    17
         See, e.g., Gov. Shapiro Answer at 10; Public Interest Organizations Comments at 19 (“PIOs Comments).
    18
         Gov. Shapiro Answer at 7.

                                                            -8-
 pursuant to Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) rules.” 19 Those two statements cannot be

squared.       Indeed, as Governor Shapiro’s filing acknowledges, load reductions are based

exclusively and entirely on the characteristics of retail customers in the zone—not the

characteristics of the LSE or ED. That is impermissible targeting of retail customers, plain and

simple.

          Nor is it correct that IRAS “focus[es] on zones or areas projected to have capacity shortfalls

in real-time—through the existence of non-capacity backed large loads in the planning horizon.” 20

As explained above, IRAS does not focus on zones or areas with shortfalls and instead turns solely

on the characteristics of individual retail customers. Indeed, an LSE/ED could be net long, with

sufficient capacity to serve all of the loads in its footprint, but if a new large load comes online

without offsetting capacity, that LSE would still receive a curtailment instruction. In other words,

the characteristics and practices of a single retail customer would dictate the wholesale service

available to the LSE.

           Similarly, the Public Interest Organizations (“PIOs”) contend that “PJM will respect

jurisdictional boundaries by directing IRAS Actions at the wholesale level. PJM will never curtail

individual retail customers—instead, it uses the Registry and results from the most recent BRA to

designate megawatt quantities of IRAS curtailment by zone.” 21                This argument actually

underscores how IRAS targets retail customers. Indeed, the Registry, in fact, helps ensure that

IRAS is “aimed” at “the correct customers”—i.e., specific retail customers without Bring Your

Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) arrangements. Or, as the PIOs put it, “[b]y tracking individual




   19
        Gov. Shapiro Answer at 8.
   20
        Id. at 9.
   21
        PIOs Comments at 19.

                                                       -9-
 large loads and BYONC arrangements, the Registry helps ensure that EDs allocate interruptions

to the correct customers during IRAS Actions.” 22 The FPA does not allow such targeting of retail

customers in a FERC tariff.

          PJM tries a different approach to defend its proposal on jurisdictional grounds.

Specifically, PJM skips past IRAS’s targeting of retail customers when it describes how IRAS will

work in practice. PJM states that when system conditions are tight “PJM wou ld determine the

quantity of MW that load in a zone/area would need to be reduced by to maintain system reliability

in the PJM Region and provides a directive to Electric Distributors accordingly.” 23 But crucially,

this ignores the key fact that PJM would determine the quantity of MW that would be reduced

based solely on whether individual retail customers have offset their demand with new capacity.

          PJM also claims that the Commission’s recent Tri-State decision shows that IRAS is

jurisdictionally sound, but this comparison is inapt. PJM argues that, beca use the Commission

found that Tri-State’s HIL Program respected the FPA’s jurisdictional boundaries, it must find that

IRAS does as well. But the only similarity between the two programs that PJM identifies is that

both address “concerns regarding the rapid growth of large loads.” 24 But that is where the

similarities between the HIL Program and IRAS begin and end. Under the HIL tariff, Tri-State

imposes reliability impact review and financial obligations on its Utility Members to prevent costs

or operational impacts caused by serving a large load from being shifted to other Utility




   22
        PIOs Comments at 19.
   23
        PJM Answer at 26.
   24
        Id. at 25 (internal quotation marks om itted).

                                                         -10-
 Members.25 In this regard, Tri-State’s regime is more consistent with the net-short LSE-

responsibility approach that Vistra supports than IRAS’s plain targeting of retail customers. Tri-

State’s regime is meaningfully distinct from IRAS’s targeting of retail customers, but would

support Vistra’s proposed alternative of focusing on net-short LSEs rather than particular retail

customers. Under PJM’s proposal, the wholesale customer, unlike Tri-State’s Utility Members, is

compelled to take diminished wholesale service solely to address the characteristics and practices

of retail customers. Thus, while the Commission found that Tri-State’s proposal “does not present

an impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation” even though it did “affect the quantity or terms

of retail sales,” 26 the same cannot be said of PJM’s proposal.

          Parties also contend that IRAS must be legal because “actions that would be possible under

IRAS are no different from other actions” that PJM can take when carrying out its NERC

responsibilities. 27 Vistra does not dispute that PJM can initiate emergency procedures to maintain

reliability, but that does not give PJM the authority to initiate emergency procedures in any way it

chooses, as parties suggest. For example, PJM could not decide to curtail only EDs in parts of

PJM that voted for a certain political party in a particular election, regardless of how concerned it

is about resource adequacy.

          Finally, parties are wrong to suggest that Vistra and other protesters are arguing that “PJM

must blind itself—that it is legally barred from acting on information about the characteristics of




    25
       Tri-State Generation & Transmission Ass’n., 196 FERC ¶ 61,127, at PP 14-16 (2026) (“Tri-State”). PJM
incorrectly points to paragraph 25 of Tri-State in support of IRAS, but paragraph 25 is a summary of Tri-State’s
deficiency letter response, not part of the Commission’s determination. See PJM Answer at 25 (citing Tri-State, 196
FERC ¶ 61,127 at P 25).
    26
         PJM Answer at 26 (quoting Tri-State, 196 FERC ¶ 61,127 at P 66).
    27
         Gov. Shapiro Answer at 7.

                                                           -11-
 load growth in a zone or area.” 28 This glosses over how IRAS would work. PJM can and should

consider information about aggregate load growth in a zone or area to ensure reliability of the bulk

power system, which is jurisdictionally appropriate and directly related to resource adequacy. But

that is not what IRAS does. Rather, PJM is proposing to determine the quality of wholesale

transmission service based on the characteristics and practices of individual retail customers within

a zone, which is a bridge too far. Similarly, the claim that “the protestors’ position would bar PJM

from taking into consideration information about generating facilities—ramp rates, minimum run

times, outage rates, and so on—because neither the Commission nor PJM have authority to directly

regulate generation” 29 suffers from the same fallacy. The Commission can consider information

about and regulate wholesale generators that sell into a Commission -jurisdictional wholesale

market without running afoul of the states’ jurisdiction over those same generators. Because those

generators are participating in the wholesale market, regulation that considers how the

characteristics of those generators impact their wholesale market activity is “aimed” at and “all

about” wholesale market participation. 30 Even if that regulation incidentally affects areas within

the states’ authority, that is of no consequence because FERC’s regulation is aimed at the

wholesale market. And were the Commission to not regulate those generators in the wholesale

market, that would give rise to the type of regulatory gap that cannot exist under the FPA, as states

cannot set the terms and conditions governing how generators participate in federal wholesale

markets. But the same is not true of retail loads that just want to take retail service. Unlike the

generators that FERC permissibly regulates within its jurisdictional sphere, the retail customers




   28
        Gov. Shapiro Answer at 10.
   29
        Id. at 11.
   30
        EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.

                                                    -12-
 targeted by IRAS are not participating in the FERC-jurisdictional wholesale market. Accordingly,

a rule that prohibits the Commission from conditioning jurisdictional service on the characteristics

of non-jurisdictional entities would not preclude the Commission from considering ramp rates,

outage rates, or anything else in that parade of horribles.

         C. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Against Existing Resources

         As Vistra has explained, PJM’s proposal unlawfully discriminates against existing

resources in favor of new resources. Neither PJM’s original filing nor any of the subsequent

comments and answers provide record evidence that justifies that discriminatory treatment, much

less render it undue. Even IRAS’s defenders do not explain why new and existing resources are

different in any respects that are material to the inquiry at hand —i.e., that they contribute

differently to resource adequacy—such that discriminating against existing resources is “due.”

         PJM blithely asserts that IRAS is not unduly discriminatory against existing generators

because “[t]he PJM Region needs new capacity.” 31 Vistra agrees, but a construct designed to

attract new capacity without sufficient attention to retaining existing capacity may even make

matters worse. As the Commission has explained, “[b]oth new entry and retention of existing

efficient capacity are necessary to ensure reliability and both should receive the same price so that

the price signals are not skewed in f avor of new entry.” 32 A MW of existing supply does as much

to maintain resource adequacy as a MW of new supply. That is an issue of physics, not policy,

and so it is unsurprising that nothing in the record calls this fundamental fact into question. In

requiring balance between supply and demand, the system does not (and cannot) distinguish

between the in-service dates of the resource providing the supply. A single-minded focus on



   31
        PJM Answer at 44.
   32
        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 128 FERC ¶ 61,157, at P 102 (2009).

                                                       -13-
 incentivizing new entry that comes at the cost of driving existing capacity into retirement will not

help PJM’s resource adequacy issues—it will exacerbate them.

           Governor Shapiro’s filing attempts to distinguish new and existing generation on the basis

that existing generators have previously received capacity market commitments and customers

have previously contributed to the “embedded costs” of those generators. 33 These arguments are

contradicted by the most basic principles of PJM’s capacity market. The use of the phrase

“embedded costs” reveals the misguided focus of Governor Shapiro’s filing. “Embedded costs”

is an established term relevant to monopoly utilities to describe the combined capital, operations,

and maintenance costs associated with a resource that a utility is including in its regulated rate

base. In a monopoly utility setting, captive customers are obligated to ensure full recovery of

resource costs, including a guaranteed rate of return, and thus it is fair to consider generation

resources as having been paid for and thus entitled to existing customers. Competitive generators

sell capacity for a specific delivery year. 34 Doing so does not obligate the generator to continue to

be a capacity resource after that delivery year 35 nor does it obligate any captive customer to

guarantee the generator fully recover its costs including a return on equity. Nor does it entitle PJM

(or any loads) to any “special equitable claim [to that capacity] in perpetuity.” 36 Indeed, arguments

to the contrary disregard the fact that independent generators provide services through volun tary

 participation in the markets and amount to the unprecedented and unconstitutional assertion that

existing load has a property right in existing generation. 37

          The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (“NJBPU”) argues that new capacity resources

should be favored because they “require additional price certainty to enter PJM’s uncertain

investment environment, take on risks from federal regulatory uncertainty, and undergo longer

project development timelines due to supply constraints and siting and permitting delays.” 38 There

are at least three flaws with that argument. First, it ignores the fact that new resources have been

entering the nation’s organized capacity markets for many years without “additional price

certainty.” Second, to the extent “additional price certainty” is a virtue, it is one that also benefits

existing resources which need ongoing investments for maintenance and refueling in order to

continue providing capacity. Third, NJBPU fails to recognize that constant tinkering with the

market, including via interventions like IRAS, artificially skews prices (e.g., by removing certain

new large loads from the Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) Curve), which undermines

price certainty for all resources—new and existing. Neither NJBPU nor any other party has

attempted to quantify and compare the alleged benefits of providing “additional price certainty” to

new resources with the unavoidable and well-understood costs of IRAS’s extreme market

intervention, including potentially the cost of replacing the resources that IRAS could incentivize

to retire. NJBPU is, therefore, wrong to suggest that the BYONC construct will help attract new

resources by providing price certainty. If anything, IRAS signals to developers that the rules of the

       U.S. Const. amend. V; Duquesne Light Co. v. Barasch, 488 U.S. 299, 299 (1989) (“If the rate does not afford
sufficient compensation, the State has taken the use of utility property without paying just compensation and so
violated the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.”).
    38
         NJBPU Comments at 6.

 game in PJM will continue to be shuffled and reshuffled with little-to-no regard for the effects on

existing contracts and commercial arrangements, actually discouraging new investment.

          D. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Against New Large Loads

          As Vistra demonstrated in its initial comments, IRAS discriminates against New Large

Loads. Certain commenters attempt to claim otherwise using three arguments. None of those

arguments are sound.

          First, some parties try to justify discrimination between new and existing large loads,

arguing that New Large Loads are solely or disproportionately responsible for the region’s

resource adequacy shortfall. 39 But no party has explained why this is the case. Nor could they:

according to economic principles espoused by the D.C. Circuit, eve ry user of the transmission

system is economically marginal, meaning that increases in demand can be attributed to every

user, both new and existing. 40

          Second, Governor Shapiro’s filing asserts that any differential treatment between new and

existing large loads is simply due to the fact that IRAS applies on a forward-looking basis.41 That

argument is contradicted by the IRAS proposal itself: the IRAS on/off switch makes clear that

IRAS does not apply to all new large loads. Under IRAS, “new” is a term of art that is dictated by

variables independent of the load’s vintage or characteristics. Whether IRAS applies to a given

large load is not a function of whether it was online as of the IRAS effective date (i.e., how a

           E. PJM’s Proposed Curtailment Priority Scheme Is Unjust and Unreasonable

response resources providing capacity are paid the same price as every other capacity resource and

capacity. It would be entirely novel to structure PJM’s curtailment regime to increase the
